channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Targeted scan detects hidden multiple myeloma missed by standard imaging
item.description: A targeted immunoPET scan detected active multiple myeloma that standard PET/CT scans and blood tests missed, a finding that could help doctors more accurately map disease, guide treatment decisions and confirm whether cancer remains after therapy. The phase 2 clinical trial was led by researchers at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

item.title: New study of Medicare 'ExRad' quality measure data shows wide variations in CT scan radiation dose
item.description: The first study to examine how imaging facilities perform on the new Medicare "ExRad" measure shows that radiation doses used for the same type of CT scan vary widely from one facility to the next.

item.title: A doctor's take: When the diagnosis isn't right: What you need to know about misdiagnosis
item.description: Getting the right diagnosis isn't always easy. Some illnesses develop slowly, some have vague symptoms and many can be mistaken for something else.

item.title: Earlier bedtime linked to greater weight loss in prediabetes trial
item.description: Going to bed earlier is associated with weight loss in people with prediabetes, according to a randomized controlled trial led by researchers at NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing.

item.title: Engineered probiotic senses inflammation and helps repair the gut in mice
item.description: Inflammatory bowel disease damages the lining that separates the gut's contents from the rest of the body. Calming the inflammation is only part of the treatment challenge, however—that protective barrier also needs to heal.

item.title: Why people trust weight‑loss drug advice on social media, even when it may be misleading
item.description: Imagine scrolling through social media and seeing dramatic weight-loss results from people taking Mounjaro, Wegovy or Ozempic. They share photographs, discuss side effects and recommend ways to get the best results.

item.title: Sunscreen myths explained: The truth about beef tallow, cancer and vitamin D
item.description: Some people are so worried about sunscreen that they're swapping SPF 50 for beef tallow. Yes, the fat traditionally used to make roasted potatoes is now being promoted online as something you can spread on your skin before going into the sun.

item.title: Diabetic foot ulcers can cause severe pain despite numbness, patients report
item.description: Diabetes-related foot ulcers are often associated with numbness in the feet. According to patients, the fact that these ulcers can also cause severe and unpredictable pain does not receive sufficient attention within the health care system, a doctoral thesis from the University of Gothenburg reports.

item.title: What if AI came with a nutrition label? A new framework measures AI's impact on human well-being
item.description: Nutrition labels have long helped consumers understand what they're putting into their bodies. Now, a new framework applies a similar approach to AI, giving people a clearer view of how the AI models they use may affect their well-being.

item.title: Nearly 1 in 5 people in the US think about food even when they are not hungry
item.description: "Food noise" refers to intrusive thoughts about and cravings for food, whether or not a person is hungry. The phenomenon has become widely discussed on social media, in traditional media and in commercials for GLP-1 receptor agonist weight-loss medications. Because the term has only emerged in recent years, not much is known about who experiences food noise, and there is not even a universally accepted scientific definition.

item.title: Teaching seniors to master the art of falling safely
item.description: Judo and elder care may seem like an unlikely matchup, but allied health professionals are learning how to help older Australians fall more safely by using techniques adapted from the martial art.

item.title: Slow brain rhythms do more than reflect sleep—they help trigger it, fruit fly study suggests
item.description: For most animals, the need for sleep gradually increases during waking hours and then decreases while sleeping. In neuroscience, this accumulating need to sleep is known as sleep pressure.

item.title: New research collects recommendations for bone-anchored prosthetic limbs
item.description: Osseointegration is a reconstructive surgery for patients in which a prosthetic implant is connected directly to the bone. The field has advanced significantly in recent years, with research showing potentially numerous benefits for patients over traditional socket prostheses.

item.title: Novel imaging modality accurately assesses lung function in cancer patients
item.description: Patients with early-stage lung cancer undergo surgery unless preoperative evaluation reveals poor lung function, which is predictive of poor outcomes. Imaging—like MRI or CT scans—isn't the standard of care for conventional evaluation due to issues like cost, the need for contrast and inaccuracy.

item.title: WHO urged to review drinking water standards amid nitrate health fears
item.description: Dozens of global health and environmental organizations called on the World Health Organization on Tuesday to revise decades-old standards for nitrate levels in drinking water, arguing they do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.

item.title: Child dies of measles in New York's first such death in 30 years
item.description: A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state's first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday.

item.title: Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle
item.description: A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

item.title: Can Australia's social welfare system handle future aged care needs?
item.description: As Australia's population ages, nine in 10 older Australians applying for aged care receive social welfare payments. Researchers from Flinders University and the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) have conducted a new study that examined the financial circumstances, sources of income and homeownership of more than 920,000 older people (average age 82) who applied for aged care between 2010 and 2019.

item.title: Toddler snacks pulled from Costco, Target, Walmart and other stores over choking danger
item.description: Parents and caregivers should stop serving Once Upon a Farm Tractor Wheels toddler bars right away because they could cause deadly choking, federal health officials warn.

item.title: Scientists estimate drownings cost the UK almost £1 billion a year
item.description: Drownings are taking a toll on the U.K., not just on grieving families but on the country's finances, a new study has found.

item.title: Australian survey reveals 60% eat raw fish or seafood, prompting safety warnings
item.description: Ahead of Australian Food Safety Week, Nov. 7 to 14, 2026, with the theme "Raw food know the risk," the Food Safety Information Council has released new research showing 60% of Aussies consume raw fish or seafood, and 17% do so at least once a week.

item.title: ASN: Elderly with chronic kidney disease benefit from SGLT2 inhibitors
item.description: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors show significant benefits for adults aged 80 years and older with chronic kidney disease (CKD), according to a study presented at Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.

item.title: The invisible global health workforce: Why nurses matter more than ever
item.description: Nurses may be one of the most important parts of the health care workforce—yet their contribution is overlooked, according to a new paper examining the profession's place in the growing "One Health" movement to connect human, animal and environmental health.

item.title: AI measurements of heart scans more strongly linked to patient survival than clinician measurements
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) measurements of heart function from MRI scans are more strongly linked to how long patients live after their scan than measurements made by clinicians, suggesting that AI could provide a useful first-line approach to measuring heart function. This is according to research led by City St George's, University of London and University College London, and published in The Lancet Digital Health.

item.title: Natural plant compound may help overcome cancer drug resistance
item.description: A natural plant compound may help overcome a built-in defense that allows many cancers to resist a class of drugs designed to restore normal gene activity, according to a study by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center.

item.title: A surge in brain connections fine-tunes visual responses within days of eyes opening, study finds
item.description: Our brain's wiring is shaped both by genes and what we experience, and the visual system is a great model for studying how the two work together. Before the eyes ever open, genetic programs lay down a first draft of the brain's visual circuits. But once they open, experience takes over, with visual information refining the initial draft.

item.title: Reducing hallucinations in schizophrenia with focused ultrasound: First-in-human clinical trial begins
item.description: Auditory hallucinations—or hearing voices that others do not hear—affect more than 70% of people with schizophrenia. Despite treatment with antipsychotic medications, approximately 40% continue to experience persistent hallucinations. For these patients, new treatment approaches are urgently needed.

item.title: No neuralyzer needed: The molecular pathways and circuit that trigger forgetting in C. elegans
item.description: In the 1997 film "Men in Black," one of the prominent pieces of alien technology the main characters use in their work to police extraterrestrial activity on Earth was the neuralyzer. This flashy handheld device would erase the witnesses' memories of their close encounter. For as long as human inquiry has existed, people have tried to understand how and why we remember and forget. As we have begun to understand how the brain works, researchers have slowly uncovered the biological mechanisms underlying memory.

item.title: A single protein that helps drive responses to touch, temperature, pain and itch could offer a new drug target
item.description: A light brush, a hot surface and an irritating itch all activate different sensory pathways, yet researchers have determined that, in mice, these otherwise distinct responses share a molecular helper. A team led by Bailong Xiao at Tsinghua University found that removing the protein CRELD1 weakened the animals' reactions to touch, heat, cold, painful pressure and itch. But how can one protein influence so many different sensations?

item.title: How an innate immune protein can control cholesterol, tumor growth and response to cancer therapy
item.description: Scientists at the University of North Carolina Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center have discovered an unexpected role for a key innate immune protein, revealing how it helps regulate cholesterol levels inside cells and influences tumor growth and treatment response. The findings shed new light on how cancer cells rewire their metabolism—and point to potential new strategies for therapy.
